# Machine-learning models: model cards

```bash
pip install -r requirements-analytics.txt
python ml/train_all.py            # trains and evaluates all five (about 10 s), writes RESULTS.md, results/, figures/
```

**Results:** [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md) is generated by the script, so the numbers always match the code.

Rules followed by every model:
- **Time-based split.** Train on the first two thirds of each 180-day run (December–March) and test on
  the last third (April–May), never a random split.
- **No leakage.** Only information available when the decision is made. The simulation's hidden
  variables (aged-load flag, worker skill in the demand model…) are not features.
- **An honest baseline.** Each model is compared with the simple method a distribution center actually
  uses, and both are scored on the same test days.
- **Money with stated assumptions.** The value per day is the model's net benefit minus the baseline's.
  Every assumption is listed below, and a result is reported even when the model loses.

Because the data is simulated, the true causes are known ([DATA_DICTIONARY.md](../DATA_DICTIONARY.md),
"How the data is generated"). A model that finds the real mechanism, and not an artefact, is the check.

---

## 1. Demand forecast (`demand.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | How many cases to order from the plants for tomorrow, and how much picking work to plan |
| **Unit** | Store × SKU × departure day (48 × 15 series); also summed per SKU and for the whole network |
| **Features** | Lags 1, 7 and 14 days, mean of the same weekday over 4 weeks, 7- and 28-day means, weekday, season flags (Christmas, post-Christmas lull, BBQ), store kind and size, product category, next-day temperature (the simulated actual temperature stands in for a weather forecast) |
| **Model** | `HistGradientBoostingRegressor`, Poisson loss (counts) |
| **Baseline** | Same weekday last week |
| **Metric** | WAPE (sum of absolute errors / sum of actuals) |
| **$ assumption** | Conservative: only under-forecast cases (stock a store would not get) are valued, at the $12 short-shipment penalty. Over-forecasts (excess stock, spoilage risk) are counted in cases, not in dollars. |
| **Limits** | Individual store orders carry ±35 % noise by design, so about 28 % WAPE is the floor at store × SKU level. Rush orders are excluded (unforecastable by definition). |

## 2. Labour planning (`labour.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Picker-hours to schedule each day |
| **Method** | (1) A capacity curve: a logistic regression of the share of late orders against picking load (cases per scheduled picker-hour), fitted on the training days of the three staffing scenarios. (2) Each day is planned at the load where the curve gives 2 % late orders (about 86 cases/hour), from the demand forecast, plus a 5 % buffer. |
| **Baseline** | The fixed crew (same hours every day) |
| **Metric** | Wages plus expected late fines per day (fines from the fitted curve, at the average fine) |
| **$ assumption** | Picker wage × average shift premium. The fine per late order is the average OTIF penalty in training. |
| **Finding** | Service is flat up to about 85 cases per picker-hour, then collapses. The fixed crew runs at about 73, so it is overstaffed on quiet days (Sunday demand is half of Friday's) and close to the cliff on peak days. |
| **Closed-loop test** | `python ml/closed_loop.py` ([docs/CLOSED_LOOP.md](../docs/CLOSED_LOOP.md)) runs the warehouse again with the plan on the 60 test days, 5 seeds. **The offline value does not hold.** The plan cuts 50 picker-hours a day and saves $1,314 in wages, but on-time drops 3.9 points (95 % interval −5.8 to −2.0) and fines and expedites rise $2,100: wages plus fines cost $786 a day more instead of the $815 saving promised. A larger safety buffer only reaches break-even (20 %: −$108 a day, on-time −0.7 points). |
| **Why** | The curve is fitted on daily averages, so it sees a day at 86 cases per picker-hour as safe; within the day the load peaks before each departure and orders miss their trailer. Each hour cut saves about $26 of wages and risks a fine of 3 % of an order's value, so the fixed crew is close to optimal here. |
| **Limits** | A better capacity model would work at the shift or wave level (load per departure window), which the late-order model already does. Hiring flexibility (part-time, agency) is assumed. |

## 2b. Labour planning per shift (`labour_shift.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Pickers to schedule on each shift (day, evening, night) tomorrow |
| **Why** | The daily plan failed its closed-loop test. Per shift: the night and day shifts do almost all the picking (waves for departures 03:00–18:00 are released 5 h before), while the evening shift had 18 pickers for about 5 % of it. |
| **Method** | (1) Volume: the demand forecast split by shift with each weekday's training share. (2) Capacity: per shift, a logistic curve of late orders against load, orders assigned to the shift that picked most of their cases, fitted on the training days of the three staffing scenarios; the plan load is where it reaches 2 % late, capped at the 95th percentile observed. (3) Crew: forecast cases / plan load / hours a rostered picker works, plus 5 %; a shift with under 15 % of the volume keeps 3 pickers for rush orders. |
| **Baseline** | The fixed crew, and a static crew rebalanced by shift from the training average (same curves, no forecast) |
| **Closed-loop result** | 5 seeds, 60 test days: 227 picker-hours a day instead of 351, **wages + fines −$3,498 a day** (−$4,853 to −$2,143), on-time +0.3 points (−0.2 to +0.9). The static crew saves $2,444 but loses 1.4 on-time points; the forecast keeps 1.7 points more on time with the same hours. |
| **Limits** | Assumes pickers can be scheduled by shift and day (part-time, agency). The evening minimum crew (3) is a judgement for rush orders, not fitted. Profit itself is too noisy between runs to separate from 0. |

## 3. Spoilage risk (`spoilage.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | At receipt: send this pallet to a discount channel now, or store it normally? |
| **Features** | Days of shelf life left and share of total (from the label), product, plant, cases, probe temperature, days of stock already on hand for that SKU, and the selling slack left once that stock is sold |
| **Model** | `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` (unweighted, so scores stay probabilities). Pooled over all five scenarios for more positive cases. |
| **Baseline** | Rule "flag if fewer than N days are left", with N tuned on training |
| **$ assumption** | The discount channel recovers 50 % of value. A pallet that would have spoiled gains 50 %; one that would have sold normally loses 50 %. Rule and model each pick their threshold to maximise this on training. A hybrid (rule plus extra model flags) was also tested. |
| **Result** | **The rule wins.** Pallets that arrive with fewer than 3 days left spoil 88 % of the time. The model ranks a little better overall (PR-AUC), but its extra flags are too often wrong to pay for the markdown, and the hybrid loses too. |
| **Recommendation** | Use the rule at receiving. Fix the cause upstream: every spoiled pallet traces to an aged load, almost all from the poultry plant (`analytics/sql/09_spoilage_drivers.sql`). A minimum-remaining-shelf-life clause in the supplier contract, enforced at the door, removes the problem at the source. |

## 4. Late-order risk (`late_orders.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | At wave release (5 h before departure): which orders get priority (an extra picker for an hour)? |
| **Features** | Order size and lines, rush flag, departure hour, stop, store kind, weekday, season, cases released for departures within ±2 h, pickers actually clocked in at release (sick calls and injuries count), and load ratio (window cases per picker present) |
| **Model** | `HistGradientBoostingClassifier`, pooled over the five scenarios (staffing varies, so the model can learn its effect) |
| **Baseline** | Flag the largest orders (same number of flags) |
| **$ assumption** | A flag costs one overtime picker-hour ($40) and saves 50 % of the flagged orders that would have been late, i.e. the OTIF fine (3 % of order value). Threshold tuned on training. |
| **Stability** | Late orders are rare (1.2–2.0 % of test orders, most in `lean_staff`), so PR-AUC moves between runs. Over five seeds it is 0.44 ± 0.06 (0.37 to 0.50) against 0.05 for the rule, and the model is worth $246 ± 93 a day more than the rule. It wins with every seed. See [docs/MULTISEED.md](../docs/MULTISEED.md). |
| **Finding** | Permutation importance ranks load ratio, pickers present, weekday and departure hour on top. That is the mechanism built into the simulation, so the model recovered the real cause. Order size alone predicts nothing. |

## 5. Cold-room early warning (`temperature.py`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Warn the floor lead that a cold room will go over its limit in the next 30 minutes (close a door, stop traffic, move product) |
| **Features** | Margin to the limit, temperature slope over 5, 15 and 30 min, 30-min variability, door traffic now and over 30 min, hour, zone |
| **Model** | `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` on every 5-minute reading while the room is in spec, pooled over scenarios |
| **Baseline** | A fixed pre-alarm setpoint ("warn when within d °C of the limit"), with d set so both raise the same number of warnings on training |
| **Metric** | Share of breaches warned in the 30 minutes before, and average warning lead time |
| **Finding** | Both catch every breach, but the model warns about twice as early with fewer flagged readings. It reads the slope and the door traffic, not just the level. |
| **Limits** | Not monetised: the benefit is avoided excursions, which the product-temperature lag already makes rare. |

---

## What I would do in a real warehouse

1. **The late-order flag** as a screen for the shift supervisor, refreshed at every wave release. It beats
   the simple rule with every seed and its drivers (picker load per departure window) are the real mechanism.
2. **The per-shift labour plan**, after a pilot. Rebalancing the evening shift alone is worth most of
   it; the forecast then keeps service on busy days. Not the daily plan: it lost money in closed loop.
3. **Spoilage:** use a rule, not a model, and take the supplier conversation to procurement with the
   scorecard (`analytics/sql/06_supplier_scorecard.sql`).
4. **Validate in production** with a pilot on some days or routes against a control, because an
   offline estimate is not proof: the closed-loop test turned the daily labour plan's +$815 a day into
   a loss, and its diagnosis led to the per-shift plan that works.
